title: Learning Lesson 4: Working Memory is Limited
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This lesson tackles the third of Chew's learning bottlenecks: working memory has a severely limited capacity, roughly four chunks of information at a time. Stuart demonstrates the limitation experientially using a Dan Willingham memory exercise — showing students a list of random letters for 15 seconds and having them try to recall it — before revealing that the same letters, reorganized into recognizable acronyms (CNN, FBI, CIA), suddenly become easy to remember. He uses the metaphor of working memory as a small sticky note in the brain to make the limitation concrete, then explains chunking as the mechanism that lets people fit more information into that small space by grouping related items into a single meaningful unit. Crucially, Stuart flags the catch: chunking depends on prior background knowledge, so novices in a topic (his example is African decolonization) are more easily overwhelmed than students who already have relevant background knowledge to chunk against, which is why introductory classes often feel harder than advanced ones.
points: Working memory holds only about four chunks of information at a time, a limitation Stuart demonstrates experientially with a 15-second random-letter recall exercise rather than just stating as a fact.
Chunking, grouping related information into a single meaningful unit, is the mechanism that lets a fixed number of working-memory "slots" hold far more actual information.
The critical catch is that chunking ability depends on prior background knowledge: the less a student knows about a topic already, the harder it is to chunk new information about it.

This explains a counterintuitive classroom pattern Stuart cites from Chew: introductory courses often feel harder than advanced ones, because advanced students have the background knowledge that makes chunking new material easier.
quotes: Today we're going to talk about something that is maybe the most amazing thing I've ever learned about how our minds work: the hackable limitations of working memory.
Here are a few things cognitive science is pretty settled on: We forget stuff that we're just encountering REALLY quickly, no matter how hard we try, and the only way to fix this is by CHUNKING.
Working Memory is like a sticky note in the brain — it holds what we're able to think about at any one time, BUT it's got limited room on it!
Psychologists have done about a bajillion studies on this, and even professional memorizers only have about four slots of working memory to work with.
So, here's the problem with chunking: the less you know about a topic, the harder it is to know how to chunk.
